ENDOCRINE__Pituitary Gland (anterior/pos:
Overview — Two Glands in One

The pituitary has two developmentally and histologically distinct parts: the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis), glandular epithelium from Rathke's pouch, and the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis), neural tissue continuous with the hypothalamus.

🔬 Image slot — pituitary showing cellular anterior lobe vs pale fibrous posterior lobe
Anterior Pituitary (Adenohypophysis)
  • Cords of secretory cells among sinusoidal capillaries; classified by staining:
  • Acidophils (pink): somatotrophs (GH) & lactotrophs (prolactin)
  • Basophils (blue): corticotrophs (ACTH), thyrotrophs (TSH), gonadotrophs (FSH/LH)
  • Chromophobes (pale): degranulated/stem cells
  • Controlled by hypothalamic releasing hormones via the hypophyseal portal system
Posterior Pituitary (Neurohypophysis)
  • Unmyelinated axons + supporting pituicytes (glia); paler, fibrous look
  • Stores & releases ADH & oxytocin made in the hypothalamus (supraoptic/paraventricular nuclei)
  • Swellings of stored hormone = Herring bodies
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Pituitary adenoma
Commonest is a prolactinoma (lactotroph); GH adenoma → acromegaly; may compress the optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia).
Sheehan syndrome
Post-partum anterior-pituitary infarction → hypopituitarism.
Diabetes insipidus / SIADH
Posterior-pituitary ADH deficiency (DI) or excess (SIADH).
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Anterior = glandular (Rathke's pouch); posterior = neural (axons + pituicytes).
  • Acidophils = GH & prolactin; basophils = ACTH, TSH, FSH/LH (mnemonic: B-FLAT).
  • Posterior lobe stores ADH & oxytocin (made in hypothalamus); Herring bodies.
  • Prolactinoma = commonest adenoma; chiasm compression → bitemporal hemianopia.
ENDOCRINE__Thyroid Gland:
Overview — The Follicular Gland

The thyroid is unique in storing its hormone extracellularly as colloid inside follicles.

🔬 Image slot — thyroid follicles filled with pink colloid, lined by follicular cells, with parafollicular C cells
  • Follicular cells (simple cuboidal) ring each follicle and make T3/T4 (thyroglobulin stored in colloid)
  • Colloid = pink homogeneous thyroglobulin store filling the follicle lumen
  • Parafollicular (C) cells (pale, between follicles) secrete calcitonin
Activity on the Slide
Active gland (high TSH)
  • Tall columnar follicular cells, scalloped colloid (resorption vacuoles), small follicles
Inactive gland
  • Flat follicular cells, large follicles full of dense colloid
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Graves' disease
TSH-receptor antibodies → hyperplasia, tall cells, scalloped colloid.
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Lymphocytic infiltrate + germinal centres + Hürthle cells → hypothyroidism.
Papillary carcinoma
Commonest; Orphan-Annie nuclei, psammoma bodies; C-cell tumour = medullary carcinoma (calcitonin, amyloid).
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Thyroid = follicles of colloid lined by follicular cells (T3/T4) + parafollicular C cells (calcitonin).
  • Hormone is stored extracellularly as colloid (thyroglobulin) — unique.
  • Active/high-TSH = tall cells + scalloped colloid; inactive = flat cells + dense colloid.
  • Papillary carcinoma = Orphan-Annie nuclei & psammoma bodies; medullary = C cells (calcitonin, amyloid).
ENDOCRINE__Parathyroid Glands:
Overview

Usually four small glands on the back of the thyroid; they are the body's main minute-to-minute calcium regulator via parathyroid hormone (PTH).

🔬 Image slot — parathyroid: sheets of chief cells with scattered larger oxyphil cells and fat
Chief (principal) cells
  • Small, pale, most numerous; secrete PTH → raises serum Ca²⁺ (bone resorption, renal Ca reabsorption + phosphate excretion, activates vitamin D)
Oxyphil cells
  • Larger, eosinophilic (mitochondria-rich); appear at puberty; uncertain function
Adult glands contain increasing adipose tissue between the cells.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Usually a chief-cell adenoma → hypercalcaemia ('stones, bones, groans, psychic moans').
Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Chronic kidney disease → hyperplasia of all four glands (low Ca / high phosphate drive).
Hypoparathyroidism
Often post-thyroidectomy → hypocalcaemia, tetany.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Chief cells secrete PTH → raises serum calcium (bone, kidney, vitamin D activation).
  • Oxyphil cells = larger, eosinophilic, mitochondria-rich; appear at puberty.
  • Adult parathyroid contains fat between cells.
  • Primary hyperPTH = adenoma (hypercalcaemia); secondary = 4-gland hyperplasia in CKD.
ENDOCRINE__Adrenal Gland (cortex/medulla:
Overview — Cortex + Medulla

Each adrenal has an outer cortex (mesoderm; steroid hormones) and an inner medulla (neural crest; catecholamines) — two glands in one.

🔬 Image slot — adrenal cortex (three zones) and medulla
The Cortex — Three Zones ⭐
ZoneProductLook
Zona glomerulosa (outer)Mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)Clustered/arched cells
Zona fasciculata (middle, widest)Glucocorticoids (cortisol)Straight cords of pale, lipid-laden 'spongiocytes'
Zona reticularis (inner)Androgens (DHEA)Anastomosing cords, more eosinophilic
Mnemonic GFR → "Salt, Sugar, Sex": Glomerulosa=aldosterone, Fasciculata=cortisol, Reticularis=androgens (deeper → more sex/less salt).
The Medulla
  • Chromaffin cells (modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons) secrete adrenaline & noradrenaline
  • Stain brown with chromium salts (chromaffin reaction); richly innervated by preganglionic sympathetic fibres
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Cushing / Conn
Cortisol excess (Cushing) or aldosterone excess (Conn) from cortical adenoma/hyperplasia.
Addison's disease
Cortical destruction (autoimmune) → adrenal insufficiency.
Phaeochromocytoma
Medullary chromaffin-cell tumour → catecholamine excess (episodic hypertension).
Neuroblastoma
Malignant medullary tumour of childhood (neural-crest).
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Cortex zones (out→in) GFR = glomerulosa (aldosterone) / fasciculata (cortisol) / reticularis (androgens) — 'salt, sugar, sex'.
  • Fasciculata cells = pale, lipid-rich spongiocytes (steroid synthesis).
  • Medulla = chromaffin cells (neural crest) → adrenaline/noradrenaline.
  • Phaeochromocytoma = medullary tumour (catecholamines); Conn = glomerulosa; Cushing = fasciculata.
ENDOCRINE__Pancreatic Islets of Langerha:
Overview — The Endocrine Pancreas

The islets of Langerhans are pale clusters of endocrine cells scattered among the darker exocrine acini (which make digestive enzymes). They are richly vascularised and drain into the portal blood.

🔬 Image slot — pancreas showing pale islets among darker serous acini
Islet Cell Types
CellHormoneAction
Beta (β) — ~70%, centralInsulinLowers blood glucose
Alpha (α) — ~20%, peripheralGlucagonRaises blood glucose
Delta (δ)SomatostatinInhibits insulin & glucagon
PP (F) cellsPancreatic polypeptideRegulates pancreatic secretion
Cell types are not distinguishable on routine H&E — they need immunohistochemistry (anti-insulin, anti-glucagon).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Type 1 diabetes
Autoimmune β-cell destruction (insulitis) → insulin deficiency.
Type 2 diabetes
Insulin resistance; islet amyloid deposition over time.
Islet-cell tumours
Insulinoma (hypoglycaemia), gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison), glucagonoma.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Islets = pale endocrine clusters among darker exocrine acini.
  • β (central) = insulin; α (peripheral) = glucagon; δ = somatostatin; PP = pancreatic polypeptide.
  • Cell types need IHC, not H&E.
  • T1DM = autoimmune β-cell destruction (insulitis); T2DM = insulin resistance + islet amyloid; insulinoma → hypoglycaemia.
ENDOCRINE__Pineal Gland:
Overview

A small midline gland projecting from the roof of the third ventricle; its pinealocytes secrete melatonin, governing the circadian (sleep–wake) rhythm.

🔬 Image slot — pineal gland showing pinealocytes and corpora arenacea (brain sand)
  • Pinealocytes — the secretory cells, arranged in cords/clusters, supported by glial cells
  • Corpora arenacea ('brain sand') — concentric calcified concretions that increase with age (a radiological midline landmark)
  • Melatonin release is driven by darkness via a retina → suprachiasmatic nucleus → sympathetic pathway
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Pineal tumours
May compress the tectum → Parinaud syndrome (upward-gaze palsy) & obstructive hydrocephalus.
Melatonin & circadian rhythm
Used for jet lag and some sleep disorders.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Pinealocytes secrete melatonin → circadian/sleep–wake rhythm (released in darkness).
  • Corpora arenacea ('brain sand') = calcified concretions, increase with age; a midline landmark on imaging.
  • Pineal masses → Parinaud syndrome (upgaze palsy) + hydrocephalus.
